## Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion — 1954 → 1992 → 2002# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/lattice-boltzmann/#1954-1992-2002
Coverage: reading

The relaxation model of Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (1954)
precedes lattice BGK. Qian–d'Humières–Lallemand (1992)
is the lattice-BGK reference. Guo–Zheng–Shi (2002)
supplies the force discretization used here. These are distinct developments.
D2Q9 has one resting population, four axial directions and four diagonals.
Weights are 4/9, 1/9 and 1/36 for those groups. The equilibrium is
f_q^{eq}=w_q\rho\left[1+3\boldsymbol c_q\cdot\boldsymbol u
+\frac92(\boldsymbol c_q\cdot\boldsymbol u)^2
-\frac32|\boldsymbol u|^2\right].
Collision relaxes populations, then streaming shifts each by its integer
lattice velocity:
f_q(\boldsymbol x+\boldsymbol c_q,t+1)
=f_q(\boldsymbol x,t)-\frac{f_q-f_q^{eq}}{\tau}+S_q.
For a force density F, Guo forcing uses
S_q=w_q\left(1-\frac1{2\tau}\right)
\left[3(\boldsymbol c_q-\boldsymbol u)
+9(\boldsymbol c_q\cdot\boldsymbol u)\boldsymbol c_q\right]\cdot\boldsymbol F,
\quad
\rho\boldsymbol u=\sum_q f_q\boldsymbol c_q+\frac{\boldsymbol F}{2}.
Density is the population sum, pressure is c_s²ρ, and viscosity is
ν=c_s²(τ−1/2). The Chapman–Enskog derivation
explains the discrete-time half-step correction. τ>1/2 makes this viscosity
positive; it is not a universal nonlinear stability certificate.

## Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion — Two independent tests# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/lattice-boltzmann/#two-independent-tests
Coverage: reading

A transverse periodic shear wave decays as exp(−νk²t), allowing an independent
viscosity measurement. Force-driven Poiseuille flow has exact profile
u_x=F_x y(H−y)/(2ρ_refν). The walls sit half a lattice spacing beyond the
outer fluid nodes, not at those node centers. Fixed τ=0.8, peak velocity 0.01,
and Ny=8,16,32 test wall placement and refinement. Startup runs for twelve
slowest viscous decay times; finite-time and spatial errors remain distinct.
The data manifest records channel errors,
Mach numbers, force settings and step counts. Unit tests also verify periodic
mass/momentum conservation and equilibrium moments. BGK is a single-relaxation
baseline: MRT/TRT, entropic and cumulant collisions, thermal/compressible LBM,
moving walls and multiphase models remain extensions. Projection flow
solves a different discrete system and provides another route to incompressibility.

## Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada — Reconstruction and the ratio convention# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/limiters/#reconstruction-and-the-ratio-convention
Coverage: reading

For uniform cells, let the backward and forward increments be
a_i=\bar u_i-\bar u_{i-1},\qquad b_i=\bar u_{i+1}-\bar u_i,
\qquad r_i=a_i/b_i,\qquad s_i=\phi(r_i)b_i.
The two states reconstructed from cell i are
u_{i+1/2}^{L}=\bar u_i+\tfrac12s_i,\qquad
u_{i-1/2}^{R}=\bar u_i-\tfrac12s_i.
The implementation works directly with a and b, so a zero denominator at a
plateau requires neither a numerical epsilon nor an arbitrary ratio. Opposite
signs or either zero increment give zero limited slope. These are increments;
divide by cell width only if a derivative is required.

## Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada — Five limiter functions# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/limiters/#five-limiter-functions
Coverage: reading

Each function below is zero for r ≤ 0. For r > 0:
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{\rm minmod}(r)&=\min(1,r),\\
\phi_{\rm Superbee}(r)&=\max\{\min(2r,1),\min(r,2)\},\\
\phi_{\rm MC}(r)&=\min\{2r,(1+r)/2,2\},\\
\phi_{\rm van\ Leer}(r)&=2r/(1+r),\\
\phi_{\rm van\ Albada}(r)&=(r^2+r)/(r^2+1).
\end{aligned}
This is the clipped, symmetric van Albada form, without an epsilon
regularization; other variants differ near extrema. MC means monotonized
central. All five satisfy phi(1)=1 and the plotted scalar bounds
0 ≤ phi(r) ≤ min(2r,2). See Sweby (1984)
for the scalar flux-limiter framework and Roe's compressive construction, and
the Clawpack limiter documentation
and MPI-AMRVAC slope-limiter notes
for implementation conventions. Names shared by different codes do not settle
which variables, time integrator, or epsilon are used.
Minmod chooses the smaller same-sign increment. Superbee takes a more
compressive slope and can sharpen a smooth feature into a plateau. MC and van
Leer retain more slope than minmod in many monotone regions. The notebook
lets the error, variation, and overshoot measurements qualify those tendencies;
no limiter wins every problem.

## Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada — Computed comparisons# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/limiters/#computed-comparisons
Coverage: reading

The scalar equation is u_t + a u_x = 0 on [0,1], with periodic boundaries.
All runs use conservative finite volumes, upwind interface fluxes, SSPRK(3,3),
N=200, |a| dt/dx ≤ 0.3, and final time 1. The last step is shortened. Both
directions a=±1 are computed. The two profiles are a unit square pulse on
[0.2,0.4] and sin(2πx). Initial and reference values are exact cell averages,
including partially covered square-pulse cells and the sine's sinc factor.
Displayed L1 errors use those cell averages. Periodic total variation includes
the last-to-first cell jump; mass is dx times the sum. Maximum TV uses every
saved full-step diagnostic, including the initial state.
The first-order comparison has zero slope. The unlimited comparison uses the
centered slope (a+b)/2 with the same flux and SSPRK3; it can produce oscillations.
It is not the Lax–Wendroff fully discrete method.
The separate Sod comparison uses the existing ideal-gas setup, gamma=1.4,
N=200, t=0.2, HLLC, primitive-variable reconstruction, and SSPRK3 at CFL=0.3.
Only the slope choice changes. Its density error is pointwise, following
the existing Sod convention; it is not an exact cell-average error. Outflow
boundaries mean that the periodic scalar mass/TV diagnostics are not applied
to this panel.
Smooth sine refinement at N=40,80,160 and t=0.2 reports measured L1 errors and

## Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada — TVD is a property of the complete scalar update# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/limiters/#tvd-is-a-property-of-the-complete-scalar-update
Coverage: reading

For this scalar MUSCL operator, the stated slope bounds together with
|a| dt/dx ≤ 1/2 give a TVD forward-Euler building block; SSPRK3 preserves its
convex stability property under that bound. The executable solver restricts
CFL to this range. Tests check both signs, periodic conservation, full-step
variation, bounds, and a forward-Euler random-data case at CFL=1/2.
The same function applied componentwise to Euler primitive variables is not a
general system TVD theorem, entropy condition, or guarantee of positive cell
averages. Characteristic reconstruction and a fully discrete positivity
construction are separate extensions. See advanced limiters
for TVB extrema relaxation and conservative positive-state scaling.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/
Coverage: reading

Separate acoustic/convective preconditioning from transonic numerical-viscosity corrections. Connect a concrete Γ, a linear eigenvalue model, Mach cutoffs and dual time stepping with explicit variable conventions.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — Matrix-solve and PDE preconditioning [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#what-is-preconditioned
Coverage: reading

Left preconditioning P⁻¹Ax=P⁻¹b assists an iterative linear solve. Low-Mach PDE preconditioning instead changes pseudo-time mass matrices or characteristic numerical dissipation. Papers may use P for both; identify the operator being modified first.
At low Mach number, |u_n±a| is large compared with convection |u_n|, affecting steady iteration and low-speed flux accuracy. This is a different limit from a transonic characteristic u_n±a=0.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — Place Γ on pseudo time [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#dual-time-mass-matrix
Coverage: reading

Distinguish conservative U from primitive q and pseudo time τ from physical time t. Steady problems omit the physical-time term. Unsteady dual-time iterations retain the physically discretized term, such as BDF2, throughout the inner solve. Γ is not the same matrix as U_q.
For nonsingular Γ and unchanged R, a converged steady pseudo-time solve still satisfies R=0. Preconditioning spatial dissipation additionally changes the discrete residual construction. Indiscriminately preconditioning physical time changes the unsteady solution, including acoustics.
\Gamma(q)\frac{\partial q}{\partial\tau}+\frac{\partial U(q)}{\partial t}+R(U(q))=0,\qquad q=(p,u,v,w,T)^T.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — A concrete Weiss–Smith-type matrix [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#weiss-smith-example
Coverage: reading

For a calorically perfect ideal gas, use q=(p,u,v,w,T), total specific enthalpy H=c_pT+(u²+v²+w²)/2, constant c_p, ρ_T=(∂ρ/∂T)_p and physical sound speed a. Θ replaces the usual pressure-density derivative. This ideal-gas specialization is not a general real-fluid formula.
Setting U_ref=a gives Θ=ρ/p and recovers the physical Jacobian U_q in this ordering. Reducing U_ref toward a convective scale changes pseudo-acoustic scales. Γ, its inverse and a conservative-variable P are not numerically identical matrices.
\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}\Theta&0&0&0&\rho_T\\\Theta u&\rho&0&0&\rho_Tu\\\Theta v&0&\rho&0&\rho_Tv\\\Theta w&0&0&\rho&\rho_Tw\\\Theta H-1&\rho u&\rho v&\rho w&\rho_TH+\rho c_p\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Theta=\frac1{U_{\rm ref}^2}-\frac{\rho_T}{\rho c_p},\quad\rho_T=-\frac\rho T.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — Stagnation singularities and a Mach cutoff [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#cutoff-stagnation
Coverage: reading

A representative bounded parameter is shown below. Positive M_cut prevents U_ref=0 at stagnation; the upper bound recovers the physical system at supersonic speed. This is an illustrative choice, not a universal prescription: viscous, unsteady and boundary-aware variants use other reference scales.
The cutoff avoids degeneracy of the preconditioner near zero velocity; it does not remove physical Mach-1 flow from the domain. Too large a cutoff weakens low-Mach benefits; too small a value can impair robustness or boundary behavior.
M=\frac{\|\mathbf u\|}{a},\quad\beta=\min(1,\max(M,M_{\rm cut})),\quad U_{\rm ref}=\beta a,\quad 0<M_{\rm cut}\le1.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — How characteristic eigenvalues change [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#eigenvalues-and-conditioning
Coverage: reading

To expose the effect, linearize about constant density/sound speed and use pressure perturbation divided by ρ₀a, normal/tangential velocities and an advected entropy variable with fixed scaling. The following P is an illustrative pressure-row scaling, not the nonlinear Γ above.
For nonzero β comparable with Mach number, pseudo-acoustic eigenvalues become convective in scale. However, a matrix 2-norm condition number is a singular-value ratio, not generally an absolute-eigenvalue ratio. Examine normality, variable scaling, boundaries and discretization as well.
A=\begin{pmatrix}u_n&a&0&0\\a&u_n&0&0\\0&0&u_n&0\\0&0&0&u_n\end{pmatrix},\quad P=\operatorname{diag}(\beta^2,1,1,1),\quad q_\tau+PAq_x=0.\lambda_{\pm}=\frac{(1+\beta^2)u_n\pm\sqrt{(1-\beta^2)^2u_n^2+4\beta^2a^2}}2,\quad\lambda_0=u_n\ (\text{twice}),\quad\lambda_+\lambda_-=\beta^2(u_n^2-a^2).\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A),\qquad\chi_\lambda(A)=\max_i|\lambda_i|/\min_{\lambda_i\ne0}|\lambda_i|.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — Preconditioning does not remove a physical sonic zero [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#sonic-point-is-different
Coverage: reading

The model has zero acoustic eigenvalue product when u_n²=a². More generally, multiplication by an invertible P cannot remove singularity of A. Do not claim that a preconditioning matrix eliminates physical sonic points. Sonic singularities of particular attempts at isotropic acoustic preconditioning also require formulation-specific discussion.
\det(PA)=\det(P)\det(A),\qquad P\text{ nonsingular}.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — Transonic rarefaction and an entropy fix [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#transonic-entropy-fix
Coverage: reading

A Roe linearization can produce an unphysical expansion shock when a characteristic crosses zero through a rarefaction. A representative smoothing replaces |λ| in the numerical dissipation as below. δ has speed units; state-aware choices and fixed fractional cutoffs are different variants.
This modifies numerical viscosity rather than deleting the physical characteristic. The published acoustic quadratic smoothing is not claimed as a faithful reproduction of every Harten–Hyman construction. Entropy correction, HLLE low-density robustness, carbuncle control and low-Mach preconditioning address different problems.
\psi_\delta(\lambda)=\begin{cases}|\lambda|,&|\lambda|\ge\delta,\\(\lambda^2+\delta^2)/(2\delta),&|\lambda|<\delta,\end{cases}\qquad\delta>0.

## Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes — Checks that keep the mechanisms separate [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/low-mach-preconditioning/#verification
Coverage: reading

Test spectra, recovery at β→1, low-Mach scaling and near-stagnation invertibility on small linear problems. Measure pseudo-time convergence separately from solution error due to changed spatial fluxes. Interior eigenvalue analysis alone cannot assess boundary reflection.
Use transonic Burgers/Euler rarefactions to examine expansion shocks, refinement and δ sensitivity. For unsteady problems separate physical-time convergence from inner pseudo-residual convergence. Low-Mach checks here are proposed work; existing Jacobi scaling or dual-time examples do not validate a dedicated low-Mach flow solver.

MCMC constructs a Markov chain with a chosen invariant distribution when direct independent sampling is difficult. Invariance and adequate exploration in a finite run are separate requirements.

## Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mcmc/#model
Coverage: reading

For an unnormalized target π and proposal q(y|x), use the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability. Unknown target normalization cancels. Proposal factors cancel only for symmetric proposals; omitting them for an asymmetric proposal changes the target.
a(x,y)=\min\!\left(1,\frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}\right),\qquad N_{\rm eff}\approx\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k}.

## Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mcmc/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Propose y, accept or retain x, and keep rejected repetitions as samples. Assess initial transients and use dispersed initial states across chains. Interpret autocorrelation-based effective sample size only when stationarity and autocorrelation estimation are credible.

## Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mcmc/#conditions
Coverage: reading

Detailed balance alone does not establish irreducibility or aperiodicity. Multimodality, correlations and boundaries can slow mixing. High acceptance can simply reflect tiny moves. Thinning is not a general way to increase information for a fixed computational budget.

## Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mcmc/#verification
Coverage: reading

Check means, variances and quantiles for known targets, including asymmetric proposals and rejections. For multimodal cases report between-chain comparisons, autocorrelations, effective sample sizes and uncertainty; visually flat traces alone are not proof of convergence.

## Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC — Publication scope and related entries [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mcmc/#publication-scope
Coverage: reading

Links lead to existing educational code and dated verification records. This reading/translation update changes no scientific code or historical measurements and does not claim reproduction of an entire paper.

## Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes — Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/meshes/
Coverage: reading

A mesh describes geometry and connectivity. Cell shape and indexing are different choices: triangles may be obtained by splitting a structured lattice, or connected in an irregular unstructured triangulation. The mesh explorer makes this distinction visible.
The element-basis chapter supplies the other half of the representation: Legendre modes, nodal Lagrange functions, quadrature and mass matrices, quadrilateral tensor products, and triangular P1/P2 shape functions. The basis notebook shows these functions inside a reference cell.

## Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes — Structured meshes# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/meshes/#structured-meshes
Coverage: reading

A logically rectangular mesh admits indices (i,j) and predictable neighboring indices. Cartesian rectangles are the simplest example, but a body-fitted curvilinear mesh may retain structured indexing. Metric terms, face normals, and cell volumes then come from its geometry. Multiblock grids join several such index spaces.
The explorer’s first example has 8 × 6 rectangular cells on the unit square. Connectivity is still exported explicitly so that the same inspection code can handle every example.

## Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes — Triangles and unstructured connectivity# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/meshes/#triangles-and-unstructured-connectivity
Coverage: reading

Splitting each rectangle into two triangles changes the cell shape while preserving an underlying lattice pattern. The third example instead triangulates deterministic irregular interior points and a fixed square boundary. It uses Matplotlib’s Delaunay triangulation, not a call to the Triangle package. Shewchuk’s Triangle paper is a historical and algorithmic reading reference.
An unstructured solver normally stores vertices, cells, faces, and owner/neighbor relationships. Boundary faces have one adjacent cell; interior faces have two. The explorer highlights face-sharing neighbors, not every cell that merely touches a vertex. Labels are vertex-average cell centers; for triangles these equal the area centroids.

## Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes — Conservation is a face contract# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/meshes/#conservation-is-a-face-contract
Coverage: reading

For a finite volume K with area |K|,
\frac{d}{dt}(|K|\overline U_K)
=-\sum_{f\subset\partial K}|f|\,\widehat F(U_K,U_{K_f};n_{K,f}).
An interior face contributes equal and opposite fluxes to its two cells. This cancellation is independent of whether K is a quadrilateral or triangle. With counterclockwise vertices, an edge displacement (dx,dy) has outward unit normal (dy,−dx)/length. Signed polygon areas detect reversed or degenerate cells.

## Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes — Quality and implementation scope# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/meshes/#quality-and-implementation-scope
Coverage: reading

Small angles, skewness, aspect ratio, nonorthogonality, and volume variation influence reconstruction and stability differently. Delaunay connectivity alone does not guarantee adequate boundary-layer resolution or a suitable minimum angle for arbitrary point sets. No mesh-quality optimization is performed here.
numart.geometry.example_meshes supplies the three examples. Tests verify positive cell areas, unit total area, connected face-neighbor graphs, reciprocal adjacency, and the planar Euler relation V−E+F_cells = 1 for these simply connected domains. The explorer is a geometry/connectivity demonstration; an unstructured Euler or viscous flow solver remains future work.
Continue with ALE moving cells, SPH particles, and cylindrical metrics and tensors.

## Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes — Variable staggering is another choice# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/meshes/#variable-staggering-is-another-choice
Coverage: reading

Arakawa A/B/C placement specifies which variables
occupy centers, corners and faces on a given mesh. It is independent of
structured versus unstructured connectivity and of temporal order. The new
chapter connects the existing MAC layout to rotating shallow-water waves,
with explicit Coriolis averaging and tested Fourier symbols.

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/
Coverage: reading

The GSPH/GSPMHD notes describe a separate particle branch.
The relativistic development review follows
SRMHD and GRMHD, including CT, primitive recovery, and evolving spacetime.
Neither branch is implemented by the Newtonian planar model below.

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — Problem and units# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#problem-and-units
Coverage: reading

The original Orszag–Tang baseline is planar 2D ideal MHD with γ=5/3, μ0=1, and vz=Bz=0 on the
periodic unit square. Arrays are indexed [x,y,variable], with state
q=(ρ,mx,my,E,Bx,By,ψ) and
E=p/(γ-1)+ρ(vx²+vy²)/2+(Bx²+By²)/2.
The Orszag–Tang initial condition is
\rho=\frac{25}{36\pi},\quad p=\frac5{12\pi},\quad
\mathbf v=(-\sin2\pi y,\sin2\pi x),\quad
\mathbf B=\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi}}(-\sin2\pi y,\sin4\pi x).
This is a widely used compressible-test normalization, rather than a complete
reproduction of the original incompressible MHD study by
Orszag–Tang (1979).
The MASCLET paper is one reference for
this compressible normalization.

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — CT: share the same edge electric field# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#ct-share-the-same-edge-electric-field
Coverage: reading

Store normal magnetic components on cell faces and update both directions
with a shared corner Ez: for example, Bx <- Bx - Δt D_y Ez and
By <- By + Δt D_x Ez. The corresponding divergence update contains
-D_xD_y Ez+D_yD_x Ez=0, preserving the matching discrete divergence.
This edition uses a simple flux-CT construction with arithmetic averages of
electric fields from Rusanov face fluxes. Face Riemann problems use a single
normal magnetic field; interface energy is adjusted to preserve primitive
pressure. After each update, cell-centered fields are averaged from faces.
Total energy is not reset nonconservatively. This implementation does not
reproduce every coordinate-system detail of Evans–Hawley or Athena's upwind CT.
Evans–Hawley (1988),
Tóth (2000).

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — GLM: transport and damp divergence errors# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#glm-transport-and-damp-divergence-errors
Coverage: reading

With cell-centered B and an auxiliary variable ψ, solve
\partial_t\mathbf B+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf v\mathbf B-\mathbf B\mathbf v)+\nabla\psi=0,
\qquad
\partial_t\psi+c_h^2\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=-\alpha\psi.
The induction flux components are F_i(B_j)=v_i B_j-B_i v_j+δij ψ.
This edition fixes ch=3 and uses α=damping*ch/h, with damping=0.18.
Linear ψ damping is split off and integrated exponentially; the remaining
update uses first-order Rusanov fluxes and forward Euler. The energy variable
is conventional MHD energy without a ψ² contribution. This educational
Dedner-type model covers a subset of GLM/EGLM formulations.
Dedner et al. (2002).

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — Measuring ∇·B# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#measuring-b
Coverage: reading

CT uses face-field differences; GLM uses centered differences of cell-centered
B. Records include the operator name, because values from different discrete
divergences cannot directly rank methods. With the fixed, relatively dissipative
GLM wave speed and symmetric OT data, centered divergence can remain extremely
small. OT alone therefore gives incomplete evidence about cleaning performance.
A separate diagnostic injects Bx += 0.01sin(2πx) with
magnetic_error=0.01, adjusting energy to preserve initial gas pressure.
This is not the standard OT problem. It examines divergence-wave transport
and damping while distinguishing damping from error reduction by numerical
viscosity. CT preserves an initial discrete constraint; it does not
automatically remove an existing magnetic-monopole error.

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — Verification scope# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#verification-scope
Coverage: reading

Tests check periodic mass and total energy, density and pressure positivity
on selected cases, CT divergence preservation, and GLM injected-error cleaning.
The HLLD section below adds Brio–Wu, Alfvén-wave refinement and field loops.
External reference-code comparisons remain future work. The low-resolution, first-order OT figures
are introductory demonstrations of magnetic-constraint handling.

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — Time evolution# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#time-evolution
Coverage: reading

The motion gallery now includes separate 64² Orszag–Tang CT and GLM movies. Their actual adaptive-CFL snapshot times and native divergence diagnostics differ. Playback does not supply an equal-accuracy ranking.

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — HLLD and standard wave tests# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#hlld-and-standard-wave-tests
Coverage: reading

Open the HLLD test comparisons. These new full-vector ideal-MHD
runs retain all three velocity and magnetic components, unlike the planar
Orszag–Tang baseline above. With μ0 = 1,
q = (ρ,ρvx,ρvy,ρvz,E,Bx,By,Bz) and
E = p/(γ−1) + ρ|v|²/2 + |B|²/2.
The HLLD fan resolves the contact and two rotational waves between its outer
fast-wave bounds. Intermediate star/double-star states use one shared normal
magnetic field. Invalid intermediate states fall back to HLLE and each face
fallback is counted. Miyoshi–Kusano (2005)
is the original bibliographic source; the accessible
Athena++ HLLD implementation
was used to cross-check the equations. This is an independent educational
implementation, not an Athena++ run or full reproduction of the paper.
All three tests use primitive MC slopes and SSPRK2 with face positivity
scaling. Step retries and HLLE fallbacks are recorded; no conserved mean is clipped.
Selected physical states staying positive is not a general robustness proof.
Brio–Wu: γ = 2 on [0,1], initial discontinuity at x = 0.5,
(ρ,p,By)L = (1,1,1), (ρ,p,By)R = (0.125,0.1,−1), Bx = 0.75,
all velocities and Bz zero, open ends, t = 0.1, CFL 0.35.
Compare HLLE/HLLD at 400 cells and HLLD at 800. Profiles are numerical
grid comparisons, not exact-solution overlays or a universal uniqueness
claim. Brio–Wu (1988).
Circular Alfvén wave: γ = 5/3, ρ = 1, p = 0.1, Bx = 1,

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — HLLD and standard wave tests# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#hlld-and-standard-wave-tests
Coverage: reading

(By,Bz) = 0.1(cos(2πx),sin(2πx)), (vy,vz) = −(By,Bz), vx = 0,
periodic unit interval, one period t = 1, CFL 0.35. Exact conservative
cell averages include sinc-averaged transverse fields and constant total
energy; energy is not reconstructed from squares of averaged fields.
HLLE and HLLD use 32, 64, 128 and 256 cells. The finest measured orders
for the mean absolute transverse-field error are both approximately 1.98.
Weak magnetic loop: γ = 5/3, ρ = p = 1, v = (2,1,0),
Az = 10⁻³ max(0.3−r,0) on a periodic 2 × 1 box, t = 1,
CFL 0.3, 64 × 32 and 128 × 64 cells. Compare HLLE/HLLD with each
of CT and GLM. Finite-field translation is a diagnostic, not an exact
solution: magnetic forces are small, not zero.

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — CT-Contact and GLM scope in the loop test# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#ct-contact-and-glm-scope-in-the-loop-test
Coverage: reading

CT initializes face B from a corner-potential curl. A contact-upwinded corner
EMF uses the face mass-flux sign for transverse electric-field derivatives
(CT-Contact in Mignone–Del Zanna (2021), equations 20–22).
It reduces to the face induction flux in a grid-aligned 1D limit. This is not
the UCT-HLLD construction. The shared curl preserves the native face divergence
at each SSPRK stage; cell B is averaged from faces and total energy is not reset.
GLM initializes cell B from a centered curl of cell Az. At each face, the
longitudinal subsystem is solved first:
 B_n^*=\frac{B_{n,L}+B_{n,R}}2-\frac{\psi_R-\psi_L}{2c_h},\qquad
 \psi^*=\frac{\psi_L+\psi_R}2-\frac{c_h(B_{n,R}-B_{n,L})}2.
HLLD/HLLE then receives common Bn*, preserving interface primitive pressure;
fluxes of Bn and ψ are ψ* and ch²Bn*. Set ch = 4 and use exponential ψ
half-step damping with rate 0.18ch/h before/after SSPRK2. E has no ψ energy.
This is a conservative GLM model inspired by the longitudinal solve in
Mignone–Tzeferacos (2010), not their CTU
integrator or EGLM variant. The fixed cleaning speed also changes the step count.
The initial magnetic discretizations and native divergence operators differ.
Energy fractions are normalized by each run's own initial cell-field energy.
Do not infer an equal-accuracy or matched-cost CT/GLM ranking. At 128 × 64,

## MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning — CT-Contact and GLM scope in the loop test# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/mhd/#ct-contact-and-glm-scope-in-the-loop-test
Coverage: reading

CT preserves native maximum divergence below 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ in these runs;
GLM's centered maximum is about 3.7 × 10⁻⁴. These operator-dependent numbers
have units of B/length. All published loop runs have zero HLLE fallbacks and
zero retries. External reference-code comparisons, stronger-field loop tests
and UCT-HLLD remain future work.

definitions, diagnostics and hashes and

## Monte Carlo integration — Monte Carlo integration [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/monte-carlo/
Coverage: reading

Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral as an expectation. Accuracy depends on the sampling distribution, weights and variance, not merely on using random numbers.

## Monte Carlo integration — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/monte-carlo/#model
Coverage: reading

Draw independent samples Xᵢ from a density p covering the support of f and average Yᵢ=f(Xᵢ)/p(Xᵢ). With finite second moment, estimate standard error by s_Y/√N. Uniform sampling requires the domain-volume factor.
I=\int f(x)\,dx=\mathbb E_p\!\left[\frac{f(X)}{p(X)}\right],\qquad \widehat I_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{f(X_i)}{p(X_i)},\quad\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=s_Y/\sqrt N.

## Monte Carlo integration — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/monte-carlo/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Specify the distribution and random generator, draw samples and compute the weighted mean and variance. Importance sampling concentrates p where contributions matter, while monitoring heavy tails of f/p. Record generator/version, seed and sample count for reproducibility.

## Monte Carlo integration — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/monte-carlo/#conditions
Coverage: reading

The N⁻¹/² scale is statistical and conditional on assumptions such as independence and finite variance; it is not a deterministic bound for each run. Rare events and missed peaks can make variance estimates misleading. Correlated MCMC samples need a different uncertainty calculation.

## Monte Carlo integration — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/monte-carlo/#verification
Coverage: reading

Use repeated independent runs on known integrals to examine N scaling and interval coverage. Record actual mean error separately from estimated uncertainty, and verify that changes in importance density preserve the target integral.

## Monte Carlo integration — Publication scope and related entries [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/monte-carlo/#publication-scope
Coverage: reading

Integrate x² under U[0,1]. Compare 256 independent seeds with analytic integral and variance, checking N^-1/2 RMS scaling and interval coverage. Excludes MCMC and rare events. Inputs, code, measured values and tolerances are linked from the method and execution pages. Not every general verification proposal above has been executed.
Monte Carlo integration

## Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states — Five computed movies# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/movies/#five-computed-movies
Coverage: reading

Double Mach Reflection: Mach-10 2D Euler reflection on 256 × 64 cells, t = 0 to 0.2, first-order HLL with SSPRK2 and CFL 0.4. The fine wall jet is not resolved. Read the setup.
Orszag–Tang with CT: 64² periodic planar ideal MHD, t = 0 to 0.5, first-order Rusanov with forward Euler and CFL 0.3. Magnetic divergence uses the staggered face operator.
Orszag–Tang with GLM: the same resolution and physical interval, with fixed cleaning speed 3 and damping 0.18. Its native divergence uses the cell-centered central operator. The CT and GLM plots do not form an equal-accuracy ranking. Read the MHD definitions.
Smooth isentropic vortex with original KEEP: 96² periodic Euler on [−10,10]², t = 0 to 4, the second-order arithmetic-mean Cartesian KEEP flux and classical RK4, CFL 0.25. No shock stabilization, pressure-equilibrium-preserving extension, or exact entropy claim is included. Read the KEEP chapter.
Mach-3 forward-facing step: 240 × 80 cells, t = 0 to 4, first-order HLL and SSPRK2 with CFL 0.4. Grid-aligned blocked cells represent a step at x = 0.6 of height 0.2. Standard reflection is applied without an entropy/enthalpy corner reset. Diagnostics exclude solid cells. This is a classical inviscid benchmark, not a NASA experimental validation. See the shock-case definitions.

## Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states — Five computed movies# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/movies/#five-computed-movies
Coverage: reading

Density and pressure appear together in every movie. These are rendered numerical states from the repository solvers, not interpolated illustrations or reproductions of original-paper movies.

## Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states — Actual physical times, unchanged time steps# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/movies/#actual-physical-times-unchanged-time-steps
Coverage: reading

Each movie requests 81 output times, including the initial and final times. The recorder saves the first completed solver state at or after each request. It does not shorten a numerical step to hit a requested time and does not interpolate the solution. If a coarse step crosses several requests, one state represents them. Actual times and solver step counts accompany every frame.
The production movies have 81 distinct states each. The MHD CT and GLM solvers choose different time steps, so similarly numbered frames need not have identical intermediate physical times. Read the timestamps before comparing them. Snapshot tests verify that enabling output leaves the final state and numerical history unchanged.

## Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states — Fixed scales and explicit playback# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/movies/#fixed-scales-and-explicit-playback
Coverage: reading

Each density and pressure color scale is fixed across its entire run using that run’s extrema over the saved states. Colors must not be interpreted as identical values across different movies unless their scale labels agree. The minima and maxima listed beside the player are measurements of the currently displayed state; they do not establish a positivity theorem.
Playback starts only after pressing Play. Pause, first/last, previous/next, a saved-frame slider, speed selection, and an optional loop support inspection. Speed is presentation speed, not a change to the simulation. At the nominal rate, 81 saved frames at 12 frames per second make a 6.75-second clip. All physical times remain printed inside the images.
A native MP4 player and MP4/frame downloads are also available. MP4 uses H.264 video with no audio; the inspectable image frames are lossless WebP. Video compression is a presentation step and never feeds back into the computation.

## Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states — Reproduce and verify# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/movies/#reproduce-and-verify
Coverage: reading

python -m pip install '.[movies]'
python scripts/build_movies.py
python scripts/check_movies.py
The builder writes the published frames, MP4 files, and movie catalog into website/public/assets/movies. It also saves full numerical snapshots as compressed NumPy arrays in the ignored outputs/movies directory for local inspection. Source hashes, image/video hashes, numerical-state hashes, software versions, methods, boundary conditions, physical scales, and per-frame diagnostics are recorded in the catalog. The fifth movie is built by python scripts/build_shock_gallery.py and has a separate shock catalog; the player combines both catalogs. Its full saved states are in outputs/shock-gallery.
The checker validates hashes and metadata, opens each saved image, and decodes each MP4 to verify its dimensions, playback rate, and complete frame count. A short small-grid build can be made with --quick --output <directory>; its catalog is marked as a quick check and is not the published production run.

The numerical gallery
opens with 2D/3D spatial fields, including the five movie entry points above.

## Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization — Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/optimization/
Coverage: reading

Gradient methods use first derivatives; quasi-Newton methods infer curvature from gradient differences. This introduction treats smooth unconstrained minimization, separately from constrained optimality conditions.

## Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/optimization/#model
Coverage: reading

Let gₖ=∇f(xₖ), Hₖ approximate the inverse Hessian and pₖ=−Hₖgₖ. In BFGS, s=xₖ₊₁−xₖ, y=gₖ₊₁−gₖ and ρ=1/(yᵀs). Hₖ=I gives steepest descent in the chosen coordinates, so units and scaling matter.
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kH_kg_k,\qquad H_{k+1}=(I-\rho sy^T)H_k(I-\rho ys^T)+\rho ss^T.

## Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/optimization/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Evaluate gradients, select a step length using a line search and update curvature. BFGS enforces Hₖ₊₁y=s with a symmetric update. Positive-definite Hₖ and yᵀs>0 preserve positive definiteness. Poor curvature requires an explicit policy such as skipping or damping the update.

## Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/optimization/#conditions
Coverage: reading

For nonconvex problems, finding a local stationary point is different from finding a global optimum. Noisy gradients, nonsmooth objectives and inaccurate inner PDE solves can corrupt curvature. Do not stop on relative objective change alone: inspect gradient norms, step sizes, limits and termination reasons.

## Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/optimization/#verification
Coverage: reading

Vary conditioning on positive-definite quadratics with known minima and check gradients by directional differences. On curved valleys vary initialization, scaling and line searches. Decreasing an objective does not validate physical assumptions or constraints.
Verified implementation example: adjoint-gradient fitting of the Bratu synthetic inverse problem
Next: two-coefficient Bratu fitting, regularization and identifiability — The existing general-method sections remain; the dedicated chapter contains the two-coefficient execution checks.

## Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization — Publication scope and related entries [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/optimization/#publication-scope
Coverage: reading

This page gives general gradient/quasi-Newton reading. Implemented scope is the separate Bratu synthetic inverse example: a scalar box-constrained projected-gradient method with Armijo backtracking. BFGS, general quasi-Newton methods and the broader checks proposed on this page are not implemented or verified by that example.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/
Coverage: reading

THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/
Coverage: reading

Poisson solvers and particle force algorithms answer related questions with different representations. Begin by fixing the Green function, boundary conditions, mass assignment, softening, and force operator. A periodic PM field and an isolated direct-sum field solve different problems, so their raw difference is not a force-accuracy measurement.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — Particle–mesh: mass to potential to force# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/#particlemesh-mass-to-potential-to-force
Coverage: reading

In a three-dimensional periodic cube,
\nabla^2\phi=4\pi G(\rho-\overline\rho),\qquad
\widehat\phi(\boldsymbol k)=-\frac{4\pi G}{|\boldsymbol k|^2}\widehat\rho(\boldsymbol k)
\quad(\boldsymbol k\ne0),\qquad \widehat\phi(0)=0.
Subtracting the mean supplies the periodic compatibility condition; setting the potential’s zero mode fixes its gauge. This choice differs from an isolated sheet, whose horizontal mean produces a real vertical force.
PM deposits particle masses onto a grid, solves the mesh Poisson equation, differentiates the potential, and interpolates acceleration back to particles. The example uses cloud-in-cell (CIC) weights on eight neighboring mesh nodes in 3D, a continuum Fourier Laplacian symbol, and spectral force derivatives. An even-grid derivative sets its unpaired Nyquist mode to zero. Matched CIC deposition/interpolation and an odd force operator yield zero total internal force to roundoff in the tested periodic example.
Assignment and interpolation smooth the force. The mesh Green function, discrete derivative, aliasing, grid anisotropy, and any deconvolution all influence the effective particle interaction. Accurate solution of a manufactured mesh mode does not establish accurate close-pair forces.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — P³M: correct the near field without counting it twice# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/#p%C2%B3m-correct-the-near-field-without-counting-it-twice
Coverage: reading

Particle–particle/particle–mesh adds a short-range correction to the mesh force:
\boldsymbol a_i=\boldsymbol a_i^{\rm PM}
+\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}\left(\boldsymbol a_{ij}^{\rm target}
-\boldsymbol a_{ij}^{\rm mesh,near}\right).
The subtracted term must correspond to the chosen PM assignment and force operator, or to a consistently designed force split. Adding an unmodified Newtonian pair force to an already complete PM force counts part of the interaction twice. Neighbor lists and clustering determine short-range work. See Hockney’s original P³M code description.
A production P³M solver, matching correction table, and adaptive refinements are not implemented here.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — Barnes–Hut Tree: open the nearby cells# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/#barneshut-tree-open-the-nearby-cells
Coverage: reading

Barnes and Hut (1986) organize particles into an octree. A distant cell is approximated by its mass distribution moments; nearby cells are opened recursively. Our geometric acceptance test is s/d < theta, with cell side s and distance d to its center of mass. A node containing the target is always opened, and direct leaves exclude self-interaction.
The implemented isolated reference uses G = 1 and Plummer softening:
\boldsymbol a_i=-\sum_{j\ne i}m_j
\frac{\boldsymbol x_i-\boldsymbol x_j}
{(|\boldsymbol x_i-\boldsymbol x_j|^2+\epsilon^2)^{3/2}}.
The Tree and direct sum use identical particles, masses, and epsilon. Smaller theta usually trades more interactions for lower error, but individual-particle errors need not decrease monotonically. The familiar O(N log N) description is a typical algorithmic scaling under suitable distributions, not a timing result or worst-case guarantee for this Python example.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — Multipole expansion: monopole and second moments# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/#multipole-expansion-monopole-and-second-moments
Coverage: reading

Let R point from a cell’s center of mass to the target, delta_a be source offsets, M be total mass, and S = sum m_a delta_a delta_a^T. The center-of-mass dipole vanishes. With s² = R²+epsilon², a Taylor expansion of the same softened kernel gives
\phi(\boldsymbol R)\approx-G\left[
\frac{M}{s}+\frac{3\boldsymbol R^T S\boldsymbol R}{2s^5}
-\frac{\operatorname{tr}S}{2s^3}\right].
The code differentiates this potential analytically. It retains the full second moment, including its trace; silently substituting an unsoftened traceless quadrupole formula would change the approximation. The gallery compares monopole and second-moment errors against the same direct force sum.
A fast multipole method also forms and translates local expansions, reusing cell-to-cell interactions. It is more than adding a quadrupole to Barnes–Hut. Greengard and Rokhlin (1987) are the original FMM reading reference; FMM translations are not implemented here.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — TreePM: a different near-field evaluator# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/#treepm-a-different-near-field-evaluator
Coverage: reading

TreePM combines a mesh long-range field with a short-range Tree field. A representative Gaussian potential split has
\widehat\phi_{\rm long}=\widehat\phi\,e^{-k^2r_s^2},\qquad
\phi_{\rm short}(r)=-\frac{Gm}{r}\operatorname{erfc}\left(\frac{r}{2r_s}\right).
The short-range force is the derivative of this potential, not merely Newton’s force times erfc. Cutoffs, periodicity, and softening must match the split. Springel’s GADGET-2 paper provides a primary example. The two independent PM and Tree examples here do not constitute an implemented TreePM solver.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — Where multigrid belongs# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/#where-multigrid-belongs
Coverage: reading

Multigrid solves a discretized elliptic equation rather than directly summing particle pairs. A smoother reduces oscillatory error; restriction, a coarse solve, prolongation, and correction address smoother error components. It can replace the grid Poisson solve inside a particle–mesh pipeline, provided its operator, boundary treatment, and particle coupling are specified.
The existing multigrid implementation solves a 2D five-point negative-Laplacian problem with zero Dirichlet boundaries. It is not yet the isolated 3D particle-gravity solver. Boundary values for an isolated finite mesh may be supplied by multipoles or another open-boundary construction; setting phi = 0 at a nearby box face generally does not reproduce phi tending to zero at infinity.

## Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid — Reproduce the static checks# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particle-gravity/#reproduce-the-static-checks
Coverage: reading

python scripts/build_particle_gravity.py
This creates the figure and measurement manifest. The Tree experiment uses 192 equal-mass particles, seed 17, epsilon = 0.03, five opening angles, and both moment orders. Its error is ||a_tree−a_direct||₂ / ||a_direct||₂. Counts of accepted nodes and direct pairs are reported; their operation costs differ, so their sum is not a timing comparison.
The PM test uses a 24³ periodic mesh. A separate density 1+0.2 cos(2 pi x) has potential −0.2 cos(2 pi x)/pi for G = 1. Tests cover CIC mass conservation, periodic wrapping, constant interpolation, self-force, net force, the manufactured Poisson mode, exact Tree opening at theta = 0, and selected force-error refinements. A target-by-target approximate Tree need not preserve pairwise momentum exactly; the manifest records a net-force diagnostic.

## Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics — Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particles-sph/
Coverage: reading

Lagrangian particles carry quantities while moving with a flow. SPH replaces a field value or derivative by a local kernel-weighted particle sum. The independent early papers by Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and Lucy (1977) are historical starting points. The static reconstruction below does not reproduce their stellar calculations.

## Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics — From an integral to particles# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particles-sph/#from-an-integral-to-particles
Coverage: reading

A smoothed field is approximated by
f_h(x)=\int f(x')W(x-x',h)\,dx'
\approx\sum_b \frac{m_b}{\rho_b} f_b W(x-x_b,h).
The volume weight m_b/rho_b matters. Smoothing length h is a kernel scale, not necessarily the particle spacing. Compact support defines the neighbor search; it does not impose a fixed mesh connectivity.
Our one-dimensional example uses the normalized cubic spline, with q = |x|/h:
W(x,h)=\frac{2}{3h}\begin{cases}
1-\frac32q^2+\frac34q^3,&0\le q<1,\\
\frac14(2-q)^3,&1\le q<2,\\
0,&q\ge2.
\end{cases}
This prefactor is one-dimensional. Two- and three-dimensional kernels require different normalization constants.

## Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics — Partition of unity and correction# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particles-sph/#partition-of-unity-and-correction
Coverage: reading

The raw sum of particle volumes times W need not equal one on a discrete particle set. A Shepard-normalized interpolant divides by that sum. It reproduces a constant wherever the denominator is nonzero, but this interpolation correction alone does not establish conservative dynamics, linear consistency, or stable pressure forces.
import numpy as np
from numart.geometry import sph_reconstruct
p = (np.arange(64) + 0.5) / 64
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 201)
f, partition = sph_reconstruct(x, p, np.sin(2*np.pi*p), h=0.04)
f_corrected, _ = sph_reconstruct(x, p, np.sin(2*np.pi*p), h=0.04, normalize=True)
The routine uses periodic minimum-image distances on [0,1] and equal volume weights 1/N. It requires 0 < h < 1/4 so the support fits the minimum-image convention. It does not infer physical density from arbitrary unequal particle spacings.

## Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics — What a fluid solver would additionally need# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/particles-sph/#what-a-fluid-solver-would-additionally-need
Coverage: reading

Density estimation or a continuity update, a consistent pressure force, momentum and energy evolution, boundary particles, time stepping, neighbor-search updates, and treatment of shocks or tensile/pairing instabilities are additional modeling decisions. Artificial viscosity used in shock-capturing SPH must be distinguished from the physical Newtonian viscous stress tensor.
Tests check the continuous kernel’s normalization and discrete constant reproduction after normalization. This edition implements kernel reconstruction only, not an SPH flow solver. See time integration for why a particle kick–drift leapfrog and a two-step first-order ODE leapfrog should not be conflated.

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — The fixed physical model and the numerical errors being tested [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#model-and-scope
Coverage: reading

The input is a simple-cubic cell of side 4 bohr containing one He atom at the origin. A local GTH–PADE pseudopotential supplies two valence electrons for a closed-shell, spin-unpolarized Kohn–Sham problem. This He potential has no nonlocal projectors. One example therefore does not validate general multielement crystals or nonlocal pseudopotentials. The geometry is fixed as a teaching configuration for convergence experiments.
The exchange-correlation functional is specified explicitly as Libxc LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN (VWN5). The label LDA alone does not align choices such as VWN and Perdew–Wang correlation. GTH–PADE names the chosen pseudopotential; it does not assert that its generation approximation is identical to the VWN5 used here. Both engines receive the same pseudopotential coefficients and exchange-correlation choice.
Atomic units are used, with lattice lengths in bohr and energies in hartree. Total energies are compared per unit cell, including electronic terms and periodic ion–ion interactions. SCF solution error, k-point quadrature, the orbital basis and the auxiliary density/potential grid are varied separately. Reducing these numerical effects does not measure the physical error of LDA or the pseudopotential approximation.
\left[-\tfrac12\nabla^2+V_{\mathrm{loc}}+V_H[n]+V_{\mathrm{xc}}[n]\right]\psi_{n\mathbf k}=\varepsilon_{n\mathbf k}\psi_{n\mathbf k}

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — Bloch’s theorem and the units of a k point [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#bloch-and-reciprocal-space
Coverage: reading

For a periodic potential, an orbital can be written as a plane-wave phase times a lattice-periodic function. The periodic function u and the Bloch orbital ψ are distinct: u is periodic across cell boundaries, whereas ψ satisfies a k-dependent phase boundary condition. Γ is the special point k=0, where this phase is one.
Here A contains direct lattice vectors as columns and B contains reciprocal vectors as columns, with AᵀB=2πI. Fractional coordinates κ give the physical wavevector k=Bκ. The coordinates κ are dimensionless; k is in bohr⁻¹ when the lattice is in bohr. PySCF stores cell vectors as rows and passes physical wavevectors to SCF. A shared input lattice and fractional k-point list prevent confusion with DFTK’s column convention.
\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r),\qquad u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r),\qquad\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)A=(\mathbf a_1,\mathbf a_2,\mathbf a_3),\qquad B=2\pi A^{-\mathsf T},\qquad\mathbf k=B\boldsymbol\kappa,\qquad\Omega=|\det A|
Sources: Felix Bloch (1929), PySCF developers (2026), DFTK developers (2026)

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — Γ points and k meshes: quadrature versus band paths [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#kpoint-quadrature
Coverage: reading

Densities and energies of an infinite crystal involve integrals over the Brillouin zone. A finite set of k points and weights approximates these integrals. This example explicitly lists all points of a uniform mesh containing Γ and equal weights summing to one. Γ is included even for even subdivisions. This convention is not automatically identical to software defaults or the half-grid displacement of an even Monkhorst–Pack mesh. Fractional k points differing by an integer reciprocal vector represent the same point.
A Γ-only calculation is a one-point quadrature of the Brillouin zone. It can be adequate for some large real-space cells or localized orbitals, but adequacy for this small cell must be measured. Γ-only and several meshes are compared with the same orbital basis, auxiliary grid and SCF settings. Different meshes need not be nested, and monotonically decreasing energy differences are not assumed.
A band path joins high-symmetry points to visualize dispersion. Giving its points equal weights generally does not produce a Brillouin-zone quadrature. This example tests integrated energy and density; drawing a band path does not replace k-point convergence.

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — The orbital basis and auxiliary FFT grid are separate convergence axes [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#orbital-and-auxiliary-bases
Coverage: reading

The PySCF orbitals expand Bloch sums of Gaussian functions. Results retain basis names such as gth-dzv, the actual function count and overlap conditioning. Increasing a basis’s zeta label does not prove a complete-basis limit; bases with different contractions and polarization functions are not necessarily mathematically nested. Basis differences measure sensitivity within the published finite sequence.
FFT density fitting (FFTDF) is an auxiliary plane-wave/FFT representation used for quantities such as density and Coulomb potentials. Refining its mesh does not enlarge the Gaussian orbital space. Conversely, enlarging only the orbital basis cannot remove errors from a coarse auxiliary grid. The PySCF auxiliary grid, DFTK orbital plane-wave cutoff and its associated density grid are distinct, and hartree must not be confused with rydberg.
The periodic Coulomb G=0 component is handled with a convention combining electrons, the local pseudopotential and periodic ionic terms. A change in the mean potential also shifts the orbital eigenvalue origin. Even the same physical model needs aligned G=0 constants, pseudopotential corrections, Ewald terms and per-cell versus per-atom units for direct total-energy comparison. Conventions and energy components are checked rather than adding an empirical constant to force agreement.

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — SCF residuals, electron count and a sampled KS gap [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#scf-and-gap
Coverage: reading

The Kohn–Sham potential depends on density, so an eigenproblem and density update are iterated. Energy changes are supplemented by a commutator residual built from the final density, orbital-equation residuals, orthogonality and electron count. The commutator measure is the maximum over k points of the Frobenius norm of X(FPS−SPF)X, with symmetric orthogonalization X=S⁻¹ᐟ². Orbital residuals use the same final-density F. Results retain iteration histories, stopping reasons and tolerances. Reaching an iteration cap is not labeled convergence.
A tolerance sweep changes only SCF settings at fixed discretization and measures the energy difference from a tight solution. This checks the remaining nonlinear solution error. SCF convergence is separate from sufficient orbital bases, auxiliary grids and k points, and from physical-model accuracy.

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — SCF residuals, electron count and a sampled KS gap [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#scf-and-gap
Coverage: reading

For closed-shell occupations, a sampled KS gap is obtained from the largest occupied and smallest unoccupied eigenvalues over all calculated k points. A positive value indicates separated occupations on that mesh. It neither guarantees the true minimum over the full Brillouin zone nor equals the many-body fundamental gap defined by adding/removing an electron or an experimental optical gap. Unoccupied states also depend on the orbital basis. A visible difference remains between the Gaussian and plane-wave sampled gaps in this example. The independent comparison validates total energies; gap convergence or agreement is not established.
F_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}=S_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}\varepsilon_{\mathbf k},\qquad C_{\mathbf k}^{\dagger}S_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}=I,\qquad\sum_qw_q\operatorname{Tr}(P_{\mathbf k_q}S_{\mathbf k_q})=N_e=2E_{g,\mathcal K}^{\mathrm{KS}}=\min_{\mathbf k\in\mathcal K,n\in\mathrm{unocc}}\varepsilon_{n\mathbf k}-\max_{\mathbf k\in\mathcal K,n\in\mathrm{occ}}\varepsilon_{n\mathbf k}
Sources: W. Kohn and L. J. Sham (1965), PySCF developers (2026), DFTK developers (2026)

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — Comparison with an independent DFTK reference in a different basis [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#independent-reference
Coverage: reading

The example uses PySCF’s periodic integrals, FFTDF and SCF. The independent Julia package DFTK supplies a plane-wave Kohn–Sham reference without calling the teaching PySCF solver. Merely changing an auxiliary representation within PySCF would not be an independent-implementation comparison. Both engines use Libxc for exchange-correlation evaluation, so that component is not independently implemented in this comparison.
The lattice, atomic positions, valence count, spin, pseudopotential coefficients, LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN, fractional k points and weights are aligned. Plane-wave cutoff and SCF convergence are checked on the DFTK side. Gaussian and plane-wave calculations use different finite spaces, so machine-precision agreement is not demanded between their finite-basis energies. Agreement is assessed against the published acceptance width alongside Gaussian-basis and auxiliary-grid sensitivities and reference-cutoff dependence. Meeting this width establishes neither a rigorous bound on true error nor chemical accuracy.

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — First-principles MD: Born–Oppenheimer and Car–Parrinello methods [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#first-principles-md
Coverage: reading

First-principles molecular dynamics (AIMD) moves nuclei using electronic-structure calculations. Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics (BOMD) converges the electronic ground state at each nuclear configuration, then integrates classical nuclear motion using forces on that energy surface. E_BO below includes ionic interactions. The 1927 Born–Oppenheimer paper is cited for electronic–nuclear separation, not as the publication of a modern BOMD program.
In BOMD, SCF tolerances must control forces and trajectory reproducibility as well as energies. Atom-centered finite Gaussian bases require force contributions from basis-position dependence (Pulay terms). Finite-difference force checks, timestep refinement and energy drift in unthermostatted NVE trajectories are separate tests. Predicting an electronic initial guess does not remove the requirement to optimize each configuration to adequate accuracy.
Car–Parrinello molecular dynamics (CPMD) propagates nuclear coordinates and electronic orbitals together through an extended Lagrangian. The fictitious orbital mass μ is a numerical parameter, rather than the physical electron mass. Lagrange multipliers Λ enforce orthonormality. The displayed convention uses a μ/2 orbital-velocity term at fixed cell and occupations. Generalization to periodic k sampling must consistently include weights and occupations in electronic terms.

## Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference — First-principles MD: Born–Oppenheimer and Car–Parrinello methods [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-dft/#first-principles-md
Coverage: reading

CPMD orbital propagation does not represent real electronic excitations as in TDDFT. Electronic fictitious motion must remain separated in timescale from nuclear motion, keeping orbitals near the BO surface. Vary μ, timestep and orthogonality tolerance while monitoring fictitious kinetic energy and energy transfer to nuclei. Distinguish the ideal unthermostatted extended-system conserved energy E_ext from nuclear kinetic plus BO energy. These statements do not establish applicability to narrow-gap systems or metals.
This section is reading only. This chapter’s fixed one-atom He example validates static total energies and k-point, basis, auxiliary-grid and SCF convergence. Multiatom He forces, energy finite differences, an independent reference and the BOMD force interface are covered in the separate From DFT to atomic forces chapter and release. Long BOMD/CPMD trajectories, timestep/SCF/fictitious-mass sensitivity and thermostats require separate validation.

Bibliographic, abstract, selected full-text and official API checks are distinguished below. They do not claim reproduction or audit of an entire paper. Full papers and third-party source code are not reprinted in this tutorial.

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/
Coverage: reading

Atomic forces are obtained as position derivatives of the total energy in a multiatom periodic He cell. Analytic gradients, finite differences of energies and an independent plane-wave calculation are compared, separating orbital-basis, k-point, auxiliary-grid and SCF effects on forces. The requirements for a BOMD force interface are distinguished from the additional validation of trajectories.

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — Forces are negative gradients of the total energy [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/#force-definition
Coverage: reading

For a fixed lattice, electron count, functional and pseudopotential, the electronic ground state is solved at each atomic configuration. The Born–Oppenheimer energy is the total cell energy, including electronic and periodic ion–ion terms. The force on Cartesian component α of atom I is minus the total derivative with respect to that coordinate. Gradient and force signs must be distinguished: coordinates in bohr and energies in hartree give forces in hartree/bohr.
The input is a cubic cell of side 5 bohr with He positions (0.37, 0.61, 0.83) and (2.13, 2.27, 2.41) bohr: four valence electrons in a closed-shell fixed configuration. It avoids a check in which symmetry makes every force zero. Directions and all x, y and z components are compared, as well as magnitudes. Numerical agreement for this artificial arrangement does not predict an equilibrium helium crystal or establish chemical accuracy. Stress and pressure require cell derivatives, separate from atomic-position derivatives at fixed cell.
E_{\mathrm{BO}}(\mathbf R;A)=\min_{\langle\psi_i|\psi_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}}E_{\mathrm{KS}}[\{\psi_i\};\mathbf R,A]F_{I\alpha}=-\left.\frac{d E_{\mathrm{BO}}}{dR_{I\alpha}}\right|_{A,N_e},\qquad [F_{I\alpha}]=E_h/a_0
Sources: M. Born and R. Oppenheimer (1927), R. P. Feynman (1939)

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — The Hellmann–Feynman theorem and Pulay terms from moving bases [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/#hellmann-feynman-and-pulay
Coverage: reading

For a normalized exact eigenstate, the energy derivative with respect to a parameter equals the expectation of the Hamiltonian derivative. This is the Hellmann–Feynman relation. Feynman’s 1939 paper is a historical primary source for evaluating molecular forces directly. The theorem alone does not make every force correct for an electronic state represented in a finite atom-centered basis. The H and Ψ below express the general theorem; they do not replace the Kohn–Sham total energy by a sum of orbital eigenvalues.
A Gaussian basis moving with the atoms changes its functions and overlap matrix when nuclei move. Even with variationally optimized orbital coefficients, derivatives of this basis dependence must be included when differentiating the discrete energy. These are Pulay terms. The overlap derivative contracted with an energy-weighted density in the generalized eigenproblem is one contribution. The driver uses PySCF analytic nuclear gradients; it does not substitute a bare electron–ion Coulomb force.
At fixed cell and cutoff, plane waves do not move with atomic positions. Finite-cutoff force errors nevertheless remain, and SCF and density-grid errors must still be controlled. The absence of moving-atom basis terms does not make plane-wave forces exact. Basis changes under cell deformation and Pulay stress are distinct from this fixed-cell test.

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — The Hellmann–Feynman theorem and Pulay terms from moving bases [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/#hellmann-feynman-and-pulay
Coverage: reading

H(\lambda)\Psi=E(\lambda)\Psi,\quad\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{dE}{d\lambda}=\left\langle\Psi\left|\frac{\partial H}{\partial\lambda}\right|\Psi\right\rangleF_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}=S_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}\varepsilon_{\mathbf k},\quad W_{\mathbf k}=C_{\mathbf k}f_{\mathbf k}\varepsilon_{\mathbf k}C_{\mathbf k}^{\dagger},\quad \left.\frac{dE}{dR_{I\alpha}}\right|_{\text{overlap term}}=-\sum_qw_q\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(W_{\mathbf k_q}\frac{\partial S_{\mathbf k_q}}{\partial R_{I\alpha}}\right)
Sources: R. P. Feynman (1939), P. Pulay (1969), PySCF developers (2026), DFTK developers (2026)

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — Finite-difference checks: smaller displacements are not always better [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/#energy-finite-differences
Coverage: reading

One Cartesian component of one atom is displaced by ±h from the baseline configuration. At each displaced geometry the SCF is converged independently, and the resulting total energies give a central-difference force. The lattice, k points and weights, basis name, FFT grid, functional, pseudopotential and electron count are aligned. The atom-centered basis moves too, so this probes derivatives of the same discrete energy including basis-position dependence.
For a smooth energy surface, central-difference truncation is O(h²). SCF solution and roundoff errors in energies are divided by 2h, so very small displacements can increase errors. Several h values are retained to locate a stable agreement range with analytic forces. A clean U-shaped measured curve is not assumed. An input SCF energy tolerance is not interpreted as a rigorous bound on the error of each energy.
Agreement with finite differences from the same engine checks internal consistency, including signs, components and basis derivatives. Both use shared functional and pseudopotential implementations, so this alone is not an independent physical reference. A separate plane-wave DFTK implementation provides the independent comparison here.

Coverage: reading

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — Converge basis, k points, auxiliary grids and SCF for forces separately [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/#separate-force-convergence
Coverage: reading

A small energy change alone does not establish converged forces. The Gaussian orbital basis, Brillouin-zone mesh, auxiliary FFT grid and SCF stopping conditions are varied one at a time, comparing forces on the same atoms and Cartesian components. Atom ordering and axes are fixed. Summaries use an L∞-type maximum absolute component norm, distinct from a per-atom vector magnitude or a component average.
Increasing a basis’s zeta label does not necessarily produce nested spaces or monotonic force changes. Nor are all k meshes nested. The final pair of settings is compared with a published target, without presenting the increment as a rigorous complete-basis or infinite-k-point error bound. The auxiliary FFT representation of density and local potentials is a separate convergence axis from the Gaussian orbital space.
Incomplete SCF convergence also affects forces. Alongside termination flags and iteration counts, inspect stored electron-count, orbital and SCF residual diagnostics. Force sensitivity to tighter stopping conditions is measured directly, and an unconverged electronic state must not be returned to BOMD as an accepted force.

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — Converge basis, k points, auxiliary grids and SCF for forces separately [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/#separate-force-convergence
Coverage: reading

Each sweep varies one control while holding the other controls at the finite settings specified in the public input. Basis sequences are checked separately at Γ and 2³, but no joint calculation combines 4³ sampling, the largest Gaussian basis and the finest FFT grid. Independent-reference agreement applies only to the designated Γ and 2³ cases.
\|\Delta\mathbf F\|_{\infty}=\max_{I,\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}}|F^{(a)}_{I\alpha}-F^{(b)}_{I\alpha}|\Delta_{\mathrm{basis}}\mathbf F,\quad\Delta_{\mathbf k}\mathbf F,\quad\Delta_{\mathrm{FFT}}\mathbf F,\quad\mathbf F_{\tau}-\mathbf F_{\mathrm{tight}}
Sources: PySCF developers (2026), DFTK developers (2026), J. M. Herbert and M. Head-Gordon (2005)

## From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface — Independent reference: the same model in a different discretization [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/periodic-forces/#independent-reference
Coverage: reading

PySCF uses a periodic Gaussian basis and FFTDF; the reference uses DFTK’s plane-wave Hamiltonian, SCF, periodic ion interactions and analytic forces. Lattice and all atomic positions, valence count, spin restriction and integer occupations, every local-GTH coefficient, Libxc LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN (VWN5), fractional k points and weights are matched. No fitted energy offset or force correction is applied.
The DFTK plane-wave cutoff is increased separately and its final force increment is measured. This is not a rounding-error comparison of identical finite matrices. Different finite Gaussian and plane-wave spaces are assessed using the published acceptance width and convergence diagnostics on both sides. Both engines share Libxc, which limits the extent of implementation independence.
DFTK compute_forces returns a representation associated with fractional coordinates; the Cartesian API is compute_forces_cart. Coordinate and force transformations are different. Comparisons here use Cartesian components in hartree/bohr throughout. The generation script, pinned Julia environment, pseudopotential, input and result hashes are retained. Comparing against the saved reference in Python and regenerating the reference in Julia are distinct operations.
